name: Murray Gell-Mann
milestone_by_age_26: Published the seminal 'Isotopic Spin and New Unstable Particles' paper in Physical Review (November 1953), introducing the concept of strangeness in particle physics.
early_history_summary: Gell-Mann entered Yale at age 15 on a full scholarship and earned his PhD from MIT at 22. By 24, he was at the University of Chicago where he introduced the concept of strangeness, a quantum property explaining decay patterns of certain mesons, published in Physical Review in 1953.
family_context_summary: Born to Austrian Jewish immigrant parents in Manhattan; father worked various jobs including Wall Street and a language school. Mother had ambitions for him. Family was not wealthy but valued education.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father persuaded him to study physics at Yale, correctly predicting he would love quantum mechanics and relativity. Father had intellectual interests but no scientific career.
primary_early_advantage_tags: prodigy, elite schooling, early university entry, physics mentorship
evidence_summary: Gell-Mann was a child prodigy who entered Yale at 15 on scholarship and earned his PhD from MIT at 22. His father, an Austrian immigrant with intellectual interests, guided him toward physics. By 24, he was embedded in the University of Chicago's elite physics community, where he introduced the concept of strangeness—a foundational contribution to particle physics published in Physical Review in 1953.

name: Justin Frankel
milestone_by_age_26: Created and publicly released Winamp, the dominant MP3 player software, at age 19 in 1997; by 1998 it had over 15 million downloads and he founded Nullsoft to distribute it.
early_history_summary: Frankel grew up in Sedona, Arizona, and taught himself programming on his brother's Atari. He ran his school's computer network and wrote an email application for students. After briefly attending the University of Utah in 1996, he dropped out and released the first version of Winamp under his company Nullsoft.
family_context_summary: Son of a lawyer and a postal worker/health food store employee; grew up in a mobile home in Sedona, Arizona. Modest financial background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught programming, early MP3 adoption, internet wave, product taste
evidence_summary: Frankel grew up in modest circumstances in a mobile home in Sedona, Arizona, teaching himself programming on his brother's Atari. He ran his school's computer network and wrote an email application for students. After dropping out of the University of Utah after two quarters in 1996-97, he released Winamp at age 19, riding the MP3/digital music wave. The software reached 15 million downloads by 1998, and he sold Nullsoft to AOL for approximately $59 million in 1999.

name: Ralph Baer
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Baer graduated with a BS in Television Engineering in 1949 at age 27. His seminal invention, the Brown Box (prototype for the first home video game console), came at age 45 in 1966-67.

name: Akio Morita
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (the predecessor to Sony Corporation) on May 7, 1946 at age 25, with approximately 20 employees and initial capital of 190,000 yen.
early_history_summary: Born into a wealthy 15th-generation sake brewing family in Nagoya, Morita was groomed to take over the family business but gravitated toward physics and electronics. He graduated from Osaka Imperial University in 1944 with a degree in physics and served as a Navy lieutenant during WWII, where he met Masaru Ibuka at a Wartime Research Committee. After the war, he co-founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo with Ibuka in 1946.
family_context_summary: Born into a wealthy 15th-generation sake brewing family in Nagoya. His father Kyuzaemon groomed him to take over the family business. Morita's father provided funding for the founding of Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family had been brewing sake for nearly 400 years; Morita was trained in business management from a young age, sitting in on company meetings with his father.
primary_early_advantage_tags: wealthy family, family capital, complementary co-founder, post-war opportunity
evidence_summary: Morita was born into a wealthy 15th-generation sake brewing family in Nagoya and was groomed from childhood to take over the family business, gaining early exposure to business management. He met Masaru Ibuka during WWII through a Navy research committee. After the war, with funding from his father, he co-founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (later Sony) at age 25 in 1946. The Morita-Ibuka partnership was highly complementary: Ibuka led technical development while Morita handled marketing and administration.

name: Masaru Ibuka
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Ibuka graduated from Waseda University in 1933 at age 25 and joined Photo-Chemical Laboratory. His notable inventions (first tape recorder, first transistor radio) and the co-founding of Sony came much later (1946, at age 38).

name: Richard Feynman
milestone_by_age_26: No material personal milestone by age 26 found. Feynman completed his PhD at Princeton in 1942 at age 24 and worked on the Manhattan Project as a group leader, but his seminal publications (Feynman diagrams, path integral formulation) were not published until 1948 (age 30). The Manhattan Project work was classified collaborative research, not a personal publication or discovery.

name: Paul A.M. Dirac
milestone_by_age_26: Published the Dirac equation in January 1928 in 'The Quantum Theory of the Electron,' unifying quantum mechanics and special relativity—a landmark in the history of physics.
early_history_summary: Dirac studied electrical engineering at Bristol University (graduated 1921 at age 19) and then mathematics at Bristol (1923) before moving to Cambridge as a research student in 1923. He began working on quantum mechanics in 1925, independently producing a mathematical equivalent of Heisenberg's formulation. He received his PhD in 1926 and published the Dirac equation in January 1928 at age 25.
family_context_summary: Born in Bristol to a Swiss father (French teacher at a technical college) and English mother (librarian). Father was strict and controlled the household. Modest financial circumstances in post-WWI England.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a French teacher at Merchant Venturers Technical College, which is where Dirac received his secondary education. Father's concern about job prospects led Dirac to study engineering first.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cambridge, quantum mechanics revolution, engineering-math dual background, mathematical prodigy
evidence_summary: Dirac was born in Bristol to a Swiss French teacher and an English librarian. His father's concern about job prospects led him to study electrical engineering first (graduating 1921 at age 19), but unable to find work in the post-WWI depression, he pursued mathematics at Bristol and then Cambridge. His unusual engineering-mathematics background gave him a distinctive perspective. At Cambridge, he was embedded in the quantum mechanics revolution, working alongside leading physicists. By age 25, he published the Dirac equation, unifying quantum mechanics and special relativity.

name: David O. Sacks
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Sacks joined Confinity (later PayPal) in 1999 at age 27. His founding of Yammer came in 2008 at age 36. No notable product, publication, or company founding by age 26. Note: CSV lists birth year as 1970, but Wikipedia confirms 1972.

name: Yishan Wong
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Wong graduated from Carnegie Mellon University in 2001 and joined PayPal as a senior engineering manager the same year, at age 27. His notable roles (Facebook engineering director, Reddit CEO) came later.

name: Henri Poincare
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Poincare defended his PhD thesis in mathematics in August 1879 at age 25, but the thesis was criticized as 'a little confused.' His seminal work on automorphic functions and topology came after age 26. A PhD alone without a notable publication or discovery does not qualify.

name: Enrico Fermi
milestone_by_age_26: Published the seminal paper on Fermi-Dirac statistics ('Sulla quantizzazione del gas perfetto monoatomico') in February 1926, applying Pauli's exclusion principle to the theory of ideal gases—a foundational contribution to quantum statistics.
early_history_summary: Fermi showed extraordinary mathematical talent from childhood, building electric motors and studying advanced physics independently. He entered the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa in 1918 via competitive examination, where his entrance essay on vibrating rods was at doctoral level. He earned his PhD in physics in 1922 at age 20, published his first paper in 1921, and by 1926 had published approximately 30 papers. His seminal paper on Fermi-Dirac statistics was communicated to the Accademia dei Lincei on February 7, 1926.
family_context_summary: Born in Rome to Alberto Fermi, a railway inspector, and Ida de Gattis, an elementary school teacher. Middle-class family. His mother was highly intelligent and a major influence. His older brother Giulio died when Enrico was 14, deeply affecting him.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father's colleague Ingegner Amidei recognized Enrico's talent and directed him toward the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa, lending him advanced physics and mathematics books. Mother was a schoolteacher.
primary_early_advantage_tags: prodigy, Scuola Normale, competitive fellowship, quantum revolution, mentorship
evidence_summary: Fermi showed extraordinary mathematical talent from childhood, building electric motors and studying advanced physics independently in Rome. His father's colleague Amidei recognized his genius and directed him to the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa, where his entrance essay astounded examiners. He earned his PhD at 20 and published approximately 30 papers by age 24. In February 1926, he published the seminal paper on Fermi-Dirac statistics, applying Pauli's exclusion principle to ideal gases—a foundational contribution to quantum statistics made while he was a lecturer in Florence.

name: Alan Turing
milestone_by_age_26: Published 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem' in 1936, introducing the Turing machine—a foundational concept in theoretical computer science. He was also elected Fellow of King's College, Cambridge in 1935 at age 23.
early_history_summary: Turing showed early talent in mathematics and science but struggled in conventional schooling at Sherborne School. He studied at King's College, Cambridge, where he was elected Fellow in 1935. His 1936 paper introducing the Turing machine and solving the Entscheidungsproblem was his first and greatest triumph, published at age 24. He then went to Princeton for his PhD under Alonzo Church.
family_context_summary: Born to upper-middle-class British parents. Father was in the Indian Civil Service; mother was daughter of the chief engineer of the Madras Railways. Parents often absent in India; Turing raised by friends and family in England.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a civil servant in India; mother's family were engineers. No direct scientific domain transfer from parents, but family valued education and sent him to public school.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cambridge, mathematical logic, Turing machine, King's College fellowship, Newman mentorship
evidence_summary: Turing was born to upper-middle-class British parents with his father serving in the Indian Civil Service. He showed early mathematical talent but struggled in conventional schooling at Sherborne. At King's College, Cambridge, he was immersed in the mathematical logic tradition and was elected Fellow in 1935 at age 23. His 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers' introduced the Turing machine and solved the Entscheidungsproblem, founding theoretical computer science. He was guided by M.H.A. Newman at Cambridge and later went to Princeton to work with Alonzo Church.
